headline: Forgotten Forest Experiment Reveals a Win-Win Path Forward
meta_description: A 30-year Australian forestry study shows carefully thinned forests can produce timber, store carbon, and support wildlife simultaneously.
summary_short: Researchers rediscovered a forgotten 1980s forest experiment in Victoria that challenges the conservation-versus-production debate with surprising results.
body:
In the mid-1980s, Victoria's government invested the equivalent of A$26 million in a landmark forestry experiment to test alternatives to clearfelling. Three decades later, researchers revisiting the Tanjil Bren site in the Central Highlands discovered something remarkable: heavily thinned mountain ash forests had grown trees of exceptional size while recovering all the carbon removed during harvesting—and then some. The largest trees in these thinned stands averaged more than a meter in diameter at breast height, roughly 20% bigger than trees in untouched control areas. More crucially, the thinned forests had stored as much or more carbon in their wood than the unharvested forest beside them.

The implications ripple far beyond timber yield. Larger trees are more resistant to fire and more likely to develop hollows—critical habitat for endangered species like Leadbeater's possum and the greater glider. Camera traps revealed possums thrived in every thinned plot surveyed, yet were absent from unharvested areas. The acacia trees that regenerated after thinning provided essential foraging grounds the wildlife needed.

What makes this discovery profound is not just what the trees reveal, but what the forgotten experiment itself teaches. For nearly three decades, the Silvicultural Systems Project—comparing clearfells, small patch clearfells, and heavy thinnings—lay abandoned and overgrown. Its access road became impassable. Its sign collapsed. Yet the research conducted between 1987 and 1989 at two Victorian sites remained the only long-term test of whether forestry and conservation could coexist. The answer, it turns out, is yes—if we're willing to move beyond false choices. Forest thinning is not a trade-off but a tool that can deliver wood for communities, absorb carbon, and safeguard habitat in a single intervention.
quick_facts: 30-year experiment at Tanjil Bren in Victoria's Central Highlands
Heavily thinned forests matched unharvested areas in carbon storage
Largest trees were 20% bigger in diameter than untouched forest
A$26 million investment by Victorian government in 1980s
Endangered possums found in thinned areas, absent from untouched forest
